description: This case study, by A. Pulkkinen, S. Lindahl, A. Viljanen and R. Pirjola in Space Weather (2005), analyses the blackout in Malmö, southern Sweden, on 30 October 2003, when the Halloween geomagnetic superstorm knocked out part of the high-voltage transmission system for about an hour and left about 50,000 customers without electricity, the most severe geomagnetically induced current (GIC) failure since Québec in 1989. The authors link the Swedish operating problems during the three-phase storm to substorms, a storm sudden commencement and enhanced ionospheric convection, which drove large and complex geoelectric fields. The Malmö outage came from an abnormal switching state combined with a low-set residual overcurrent relay that was very sensitive to the third harmonic created by GIC, and the paper proposes a semi-deterministic approach to forecasting GIC-related activity. A 2022 follow-up by Rosenqvist and colleagues, open access under CC BY, validated 3D GIC modelling on a southern Swedish line and found 1D methods underestimate GIC by about 50 percent. The 2005 paper is accessible online on the Wiley site under its terms, with an open abstract. Caveats: the analysis centres on one national grid and relay settings specific to it. It illustrates post-event analysis of space weather hazard exposure and cascading failure in power grids; related records are the Hydro-Québec 1989 case study, SuperMAG and SWMF.
